query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi-phase eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy, the accelerated degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures is driven by the cyclic formation and mechanical spallation of heterogeneous oxide films across the alternating soft FCC and hard B2 phases. The differential oxidation kinetics between the anodic (Al-Ni-rich) and cathodic (Co-Cr-Fe-rich) regions leads to localized galvanic cells. Under mechanical wear, the spallation of the protective oxide exposes fresh anodic sites, amplifying both corrosion rates and abrasive wear, compared to a homogeneous single-phase HEA.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy with a ~2 μm lamellar structure comprising alternating soft FCC and hard B2 phases and an initially stable passive oxide film.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous wear and corrosion testing at an elevated temperature (e.g., 700°C) in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid environment, with a well-defined reciprocating sliding wear load.
generation.conditions: Testing at elevated temperature (approximately 700°C), in a chemically aggressive environment (chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution), with controlled sliding wear (reciprocating wear test) for a specified duration.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of differential oxide scales on the distinct phases, where the mechanically weak oxide on the anodic (Al-Ni-rich) regions spalls under wear, exposing fresh metal that forms localized galvanic couples with the more inert cathodic (Co-Cr-Fe-rich) regions.
generation.mechanism: Differential oxidation kinetics leads to heterogeneous oxide layers that are selectively removed by mechanical wear. The periodic spallation exposes fresh, anodic metal, thereby accelerating localized corrosion through galvanic coupling between the dissimilar phases. This synergy results in a degradation rate significantly higher than from wear or corrosion alone.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a single-phase HEA baseline or isolated wear/corrosion tests, the multi-phase eutectic HEA is predicted to show an overall degradation (mass loss) increase of roughly 2× or more, with a higher wear depth and increased corrosion current densities specifically localized on the anodic regions. The coefficient of friction may also vary due to intermittent oxide spallation.
generation.baseline: A chemically homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with similar overall composition but lacking lamellar phase distribution, or testing the eutectic HEA under isolated wear or corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: Elevated temperature (around 700°C), in a corrosive medium (chloride-containing sulfuric acid), with consistent mechanical loading and similar environmental humidity and exposure time.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative changes (e.g., degradation rates) may vary due to subtle differences in the oxide adherence, spallation thresholds, and microstructural imperfections. Also, the interplay between wear-induced oxide regeneration and mechanical damage may introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) the conventional multi-phase eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA with lamellar FCC/B2 structure and (b) a homogenized single-phase HEA of similar bulk composition by adjusting processing parameters to eliminate lamellar segregation. Subject both sets to identical simultaneous wear-corrosion tests at 700°C in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution with controlled reciprocating wear. Monitor mass loss, wear depth (via profilometry), localized corrosion rates (using electrochemical methods), and surface oxide integrity (by SEM/XPS) over time.
measurements: Wear track depth and coefficient of friction
Electrochemical corrosion current density and impedance response
Surface analysis for oxide composition and spallation events (SEM, XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multi-phase eutectic HEA does not exhibit a significantly higher overall degradation (both in mass loss and localized corrosion rates) than the single-phase baseline under identical conditions, or if oxide formation-spallation dynamics are not observed (i.e., if the oxide films remain intact and protective), then the proposed mechanism based on differential oxide spallation and galvanic effects is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

To verify this novel alloy design strategy, an industrial scale AlCoCrFeNi2.1 ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared, as shown in Fig. 1a. The bulk AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b. The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a. Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. The coupled grown two phases showed a clear compositional contrast, with the regions marked by A in Fig. 2b were rich in Co, Cr and Fe, while the regions marked by B were rich in Al and Ni (detailed compositional information given in Table 1). Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 was conducted as an alternative powder metallurgical production technique for high-entropy alloys (HEA). A dense microstructure of the sintered parts can be achieved. In comparison to the casting route, the fast cooling rate during atomisation suppresses the segregation of the melt and hence the precipitation of an fcc phase. The samples produced by SPS exhibit a multiphase microstructure comprising two major bcc phases. An ordered bcc phase with B2 structure and a disordered bcc phase with A2 structure are formed. In accordance with samples produced by arc-melting, a minor fcc phase is detected. Furthermore, an additional tetragonal σ-phase was detected after processing by SPS. Based on the above conclusions, the corrosion process of the EHEA in the test solution is schematically described in Figure 14. The passive films of few Al-Ni-rich phases are attacked by Cl− at lower temperature (Figure 14a2), and then occurs localized corrosion (Figure 14a3); while the passive films of Al-Ni-rich phases are damaged (Figure 14b2), and more Al-Ni-rich phases are dissolved at higher temperature (Figure 14b3). Metastable pits are preferentially created on the grain boundary or B2 phase. Pitting is enhanced by the effect of polarization. Due to autocatalysis by the caustic ions, the metastable pits gradually grow in the pitting corrosion area or the selective dissolution region. Moreover, the size of the selective dissolution region increases with temperature, and pitting occurs on the surface at various temperatures.

papers.title: A promising new class of high‐temperature alloys: eutectic high‐entropy alloys.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy (HEA) with alternating soft FCC and hard B2 phases
papers.approach: Casting route to produce a uniform, fine lamellar (eutectic) microstructure that combines ductility and strength up to 700 °C
papers.findings: The alloy exhibits a finely spaced (~2 μm) lamellar structure with alternating chemical regions (Co–Cr–Fe-rich versus Al–Ni-rich), which yields an unprecedented combination of tensile ductility and strength maintained at elevated temperatures.
papers.mechanism: The dual-phase synergistic behavior is proposed to arise from the alternating phases—each with distinct oxidation and mechanical characteristics—that may lead to differential oxidation kinetics and intrinsic galvanic coupling under aggressive environments.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High‐Entropy Alloy in Chloride‐Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperature
papers.approach: Electrochemical measurements combined with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions over a range of temperatures
papers.findings: At low temperatures, the passive film on the alloy is stable; however, at elevated temperatures the passive film becomes unstable with preferential attack on the Al–Ni-rich regions leading to pitting, particularly along grain boundaries where galvanic differences are strong.
papers.mechanism: Differential corrosion is proposed to result from the inherent chemical heterogeneity—where anodic (Al/Ni-rich) and cathodic (Cr-rich) regions create localized galvanic cells—and the instability of the passive film under high-temperature corrosive conditions.

papers.title: High‐Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 High‐Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA produced via spark plasma sintering (SPS)
papers.approach: Reciprocating wear tests conducted at room temperature and elevated temperatures with careful phase analysis via XRD to assess oxide‐layer formation during wear
papers.findings: At elevated temperatures, the alloy forms a protective oxide scale that improves wear resistance under isolated wear conditions; nonetheless, when combined with corrosive attack, the mechanical removal (spallation) of the protective oxide may accelerate overall degradation.
papers.mechanism: A dynamic balance between protective oxide formation and its wear-induced removal is implicated. In a coupled wear–corrosion environment, the repetitive mechanical spallation exposes fresh anodic sites, exacerbating localized corrosion through galvanic interactions between the multi-phase microstructure.

papers.system: Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 high‐entropy alloy coated onto SS‐304
papers.approach: Microwave cladding to deposit HEA coatings followed by tribo‐corrosion testing under thermal treatment (800 °C) to evaluate the formation of protective oxide/spinel layers
papers.findings: The cladded coating shows enhanced hardness and improved tribological performance under severe conditions via formation of a protective surface layer that retards both wear and corrosion, although the testing was done under isolated conditions rather than fully simultaneous wear–corrosion.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced performance is attributed to the controlled formation of oxide/spinel phases that act as protective barriers. However, in a multi-phase eutectic system the competition between oxidation, wear-induced spallation, and galvanic coupling may drive accelerated degradation.

established: Eutectic HEAs can be successfully designed with finely spaced lamellar structures that combine mechanically distinct phases (e.g., soft FCC and hard B2), offering high ductility and strength at elevated temperatures.
At elevated temperatures, protective oxide films (such as Al2O3 or complex spinels) can form on HEA surfaces, which typically improve wear resistance when considered in isolation.

Chemical heterogeneity in multi-phase HEAs leads to differential oxidation and corrosion behavior, with some regions (e.g., Al–Ni-rich areas) being more anodic and thus more vulnerable to pitting in chloride-containing environments.

approaches_tried.approach: Design of eutectic high‐entropy alloys with alternating soft and hard phases via controlled casting or SPS
approaches_tried.outcome: Successful attainment of fine lamellar microstructures with enhanced room and elevated-temperature mechanical properties; however, coupled wear–corrosion interactions remain challenging.

approaches_tried.approach: Microwave cladding to deposit HEA coatings for tribo‐corrosion environments
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved surface hardness, formation of protective oxide/spinel layers and better performance under corrosion and wear when tested in separate or mildly coupled conditions.

mechanisms: Differential oxidation kinetics between chemically distinct phases leading to localized galvanic cells
Wear-induced spallation of protective oxide films exposing fresh, anodic regions
Adaptive friction interface protection via dynamic oxide regeneration (which may be compromised under simultaneous aggressive corrosion)
disagreements: Some studies emphasize the beneficial effect of protective oxide layers in enhancing wear resistance at high temperatures, while others show that at elevated temperatures and in corrosive environments, these films can become unstable and actively accelerate degradation.
There is debate over the extent to which microstructural phase boundaries contribute to galvanic corrosion relative to the effects of mechanical film removal during wear.
open_questions: How do the inherent galvanic interactions between eutectic phases quantitatively influence the overall rate of degradation when wear and corrosion occur simultaneously?
What is the critical lamellar spacing or phase distribution that minimizes the detrimental synergy between wear-induced film spallation and corrosion attack?
How does the dynamic process of oxide film regeneration versus spallation evolve under truly coupled wear–corrosion conditions at elevated temperatures?
opportunities: Conduct controlled experiments comparing a multi-phase eutectic HEA with a single-phase baseline under identical high-temperature corrosive and mechanical (wear) loading, thereby isolating the impact of phase heterogeneity on degradation rates.

Implement in situ monitoring techniques (e.g., high-temperature electrochemical impedance spectroscopy combined with real-time wear tracking) to directly observe the rate of oxide film breakdown and reformation.

Explore microstructural tuning (through adjusting lamellar spacing, phase volume fractions, or composition gradients) to reduce galvanic coupling and improve the stability of protective oxide layers under simultaneous wear–corrosion conditions.

directions.direction: In situ tribo-corrosion monitoring of the multi-phase eutectic HEA under elevated temperature, combining electrochemical impedance spectroscopy with real‐time friction/wear tracking to directly observe oxide layer formation, spallation, and fresh metal exposure.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the dynamic evolution of oxide films under simultaneous wear-corrosion. While technically challenging at elevated temperatures, it leverages established in situ measurement techniques (e.g., EIS, high temperature optical imaging), and well-established oxidation and wear theories support it. Its feasibility depends on available high-temperature instrumentation, and it would yield time-resolved data to correlate oxide breakdown with degradation spikes.

directions.direction: Comparative study between a multi-phase eutectic HEA and a chemically uniform (single-phase) HEA under identical wear-corrosion conditions to isolate the role of differential oxidation kinetics and galvanic coupling.
directions.assessment: This approach directly assesses the impact of microstructural heterogeneity on degradation. By comparing a eutectic alloy (with alternating soft FCC and hard B2 phases) with a single-phase counterpart, the study punishes the proposed galvanic coupling effect. The physics of differential oxidation and galvanic corrosion is well understood (supported by PMC4145285 and PMC9319277), and such controlled processing is feasible in a strong laboratory, making this a direct and informative experiment.

directions.direction: Modelling and simulation of the mechanical spallation of protective oxide layers on a multi-phase HEA under simultaneous wear and corrosive attack, including finite element analysis that incorporates phase-dependent oxidation kinetics.
directions.assessment: This simulation-based approach can theoretically isolate the stress fields and oxidation profiles induced by phase heterogeneity. Although it relies on accurate input parameters and phase-specific kinetics, and may require extensive calibration, it would offer mechanistic insights at the microstructural level but might lack the direct experimental falsifiability required.

directions.direction: Heat treatment and surface pre-oxidation experiments to stabilize the oxide layer on the eutectic HEA, then subjecting it to wear-corrosion tests in order to assess whether improved oxide adherence reduces degradation.
directions.assessment: This approach tests the hypothesis indirectly by modifying the oxide properties. It can demonstrate that reducing film spallation (by stabilizing the oxide) mitigates accelerated degradation. However, it may confound the effect of microstructural heterogeneity with the effect of treatment, making the interpretation less direct.

directions.direction: Application of tailored surface coatings or inhibitors that preferentially adhere to the anodic regions of the eutectic microstructure to disrupt the galvanic coupling, followed by wear-corrosion testing to quantify changes.
directions.assessment: This direction is application oriented and serves as a means of mitigating degradation rather than validating the mechanistic hypothesis. It respects the constraints but may yield data on performance improvement without directly proving the underlying mechanism.

choice.direction: Comparative study between multi-phase eutectic HEA and single-phase HEA under identical wear-corrosion conditions
choice.why: This approach directly distinguishes the role of microstructural heterogeneity by isolating the contributions of differential oxidation kinetics and galvanic coupling. The hypothesis that the alternating soft and hard phases promote localized oxide spallation and fresh anode exposure is most clearly tested by comparing against a uniform, chemically homogeneous counterpart. The literature supports the impact of chemical heterogeneity on localized corrosion (see PMC4145285 and PMC9319277), and wear studies (PMC7515071) emphasize that oxide dynamics are crucial. The experiment is feasible and falsifiable using standardized wear-corrosion conditions.
